metadata.title: This Trump-backed drone company is competing directly with China

content.text:
Based in the US, Unusual Machines (UMAC) manufacturers first person view (FPV) drones and parts for other drone developers. President Trump's son, Donald Jr., sits on the company's board and is a prominent shareholder.
Unusual Machines CEO Allan Evans comes on Asking for a Trend to discuss China's market share in manufacturing drone components and the "bigger spotlight" the Trump family's investments has created for the company to succeed in.
We're doing the parts, so we're like a tier one supplier where there's so many great drone companies out there. We think of them like the car companies like a Tesla or a GM. We're doing tires. I mean, we're doing batteries, the power train, the motors, sort of the the things that people used to source in from China that one DI or the other stuff that everyone needs. And we're building a lot of it in Orlando. So it's pretty exciting.
And who who's buying uh these components out? Like who's your customers? Is it the federal government? Is it um is it other drone makers Allen? Is it both?
Yeah, no, and we don't really sell anything to the government directly. We sell to other drone companies. So if you look, there's like the drone dominance program, which is out there where they're government's doing this challenge to try to buy 250,000 drones next year. more than half the companies in that program are customers of ours buying things like motors and other stuff because there's a mandate for a domestic supply chain.
We've talked to analysts Alan on the show about how the modern battlefield is really evolving and really changing. Why are drones such a high priority on that future battlefield?
I think they're high priority for two reasons. First, they've been shown to be very effective in Ukraine and in Israel. and then second for the US government, we realized the whole supply chain for all of that was coming out of China. And so there's a concern that if we don't have a domestic supply chain and there's a conflict or a supply disruption in Asia that we wouldn't have it as a tool in our toolbox.
Can we put a hard number on it, Alan? Like what percentage of drones are still running through China that come here?
Uh the ones in the US are really starting to trend down. DJI still has a dominant position. They're a great company. It's probably 70% of the domestic market, non-defense. And if you look at Europe, it's it's probably 80% of the parts coming in for both uh Ukraine and Russia are still probably coming out of China.
I I'm curious Allen, you know, you saw this Wall Street Journal report, Trump administration considering funding funding American drone companies. Broadly, Alan, I'm just curious, what what role do you think the federal government has here and trying to, you know, um, increase production, scale this industry? What would be the right role in your opinion?
So, I think they've actually been doing a very good job. and this is actually started under the Biden administration when they passed like all the laws that sort of kicked out Chinese drones, they were passed unanimously. So it's not really a partisan issue. So they created a marketplace and now they're injecting the demand signal into the marketplace. So they're doing both sides to help all the drone companies really show up and and scale as quickly as possible, you know, make the market and fund the market. So, a really great job across everybody who's been in both administrations now.
Alan, uh, Donald Trump Jr. has an advisory role I read on your company. I I thought I heard uh read an article Allen where you said, listen, his role here, it's not about, um, it's about business uh connections, it's not about politics. What what did you mean by that, Alan?
Uh what I mean to say, and so he invested even before the election, but very interested in onshoring, right? Reindustrialization and everything else. and so he had a lot of great connections to the people who are also in trying to push onshoring with a lot of the things we've let go away over the last 40 years.
Any concerns you might have Alan about perception issues? I mean, you you have the president's family now, they're invested in drones, maybe some people think, okay, so could that could politics be influencing Pentagon decision making. I'm sure you've heard that and I'm just curious what your reaction to that is.
I I've definitely heard it. What I can say is it actually has created even a bigger spotlight and us have to have to be even better at what we do because people are actually leaning against us rather than for us. So we've had senior officials in the Department of War come down and tour our facilities. So many people have had to come by and audit what we're doing to validate that we're really doing it because, you know, when it comes to the defense of everybody that we care about in these physical goods, you, you kind of, you have to really do the thing. So where people might perceive it is one side, it's actually required like a just a higher level of discipline and operation from us.
